newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar falters, then recovers in Asia after G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falters, then recovers in Asia after G7.

text.p: The dollar faltered then recovered in Asian trade on Monday after world financial leaders endorsed its two-year comeback but left markets muddled over where the currency should go from here.

The dollar stood at around 123.10 yen in late afternoon trade, unchanged from the close in New York on Friday, after falling as low as 120.30 earlier in Asia in reaction to Saturday's Group of Seven (G7) statement.
It was also trading at around 1.6356 marks after ending the week in New York at 1.6610.

In a statement released after their meeting on Saturday, the Group of Seven (G7) nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- signalled their desire for stability in currency markets by saying that their currencies were no longer out of sync with economic reality.
The currency market, however, was left guessing just how much movement the G7 would tolerate -- either up or down -- before members might intervene to stabilise the dollar.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said Japan got what it wanted from the G7 gathering and that cooperative ties among group members remained firm. "In this sense, I think, under the present conditions, it sent an extremely good signal to the market," he told a parliamentary panel.

The Japanese Finance Ministry's Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his ability to influence currency markets, also told the panel that Monday's yen rate of about 122.50 to the dollar reflected the G7's call for stability.

"We have been seeking a stable foreign exchange market and have said that excessive fluctuations were undesirable, which was stated in the G7 statement. The currency rate today reflects that and is at 122.50 yen (to the dollar)," he said.
Japan has been of two minds about the yen's slide, which has more than halved its value against the dollar since the U.S. currency hit a post-war low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.
A weak yen boosts exports and so gives the economy a lift, but too steep a drop could undermine shaky Tokyo share prices and later lead to an equally steep and unwelcome rise.
The dollar rose to a day-high of 122.93 yen, but then fell back a tad as dealers lacked confidence to move aggressively in either direction.
Japanese dealers were reluctant to set the pace given a Japanese holiday on Tuesday and a desire to see how markets in London and New York evaluated the G7 stance.

Some dealers said 123 yen was a key short-term barrier to further gains, but added that sentiment for the dollar remained bullish given a strong U.S. economy and jitters over the strength of Japan's recovery and its financial system health.
Early in the day, the market shrugged off Japanese trade data which showed that Japan's trade surplus shrank 20.0 percent to 1.046 trillion yen ($8.5 billion) in December.
Tokyo share prices, meanwhile, powered higher on the belief that the yen would stay weak and boost earnings for Japan's exporters, which lately have acted as a prop for the market.
The key 225-Nikkei share average finished the day up 314.13 points, or 1.76 percent, at 18,181.17 after rising more than 400 points earlier in the day.
The market was also cheered by Finance Minister Mitsuzuka's pledge in parliament of government support for Japan's top 20 banks' efforts to resolve their bad loan troubles, some brokers said.
But they said that room for further gains was limited as long as worries remained about the bad loan burdens of the banking and construction sectors. ($1=123 yen)
